items.stem: Which term describes screen-based, digital media that are interactive, networked and allow users to create and share content?
items.answer: New media
items.markingKey: New media: screen-based, digital media that are interactive, networked and allow users to create and share content. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “interactivity”? Give one example.
items.answer: The ability of users to respond to and shape media content. Example: commenting, voting and playing online games.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the ability of users to respond to and shape media content); 1 mark for a relevant example such as commenting, voting and playing online games. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “prosumer” and “user-generated content”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Prosumer: a person who both produces and consumes media content (e.g. a teenager who watches videos and makes her own). User-generated content: media content created by ordinary users rather than professional organisations (e.g. videos uploaded by individuals).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Freya, aged 16, in Dubai watches TV series on her phone, posts her own dance videos, comments on friends’ posts and plays an online game with players in four countries. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Pluralism: new media increase diversity and access: anyone can publish, so power is spread more widely and audiences have more choice (Jenkins, Shirky).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A local newspaper in Bogotá closes its print edition and moves online, where readers comment on stories and send in their own photos and videos. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: new media create a media-saturated, fragmented world of choice in which people construct identities and reality blurs with representation (Baudrillard).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research the amount of user-generated content on news websites.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the amount of user-generated content on news websites but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the conversion of all forms of information into digital code that can be stored and shared?

items.markingKey: Digitalisation: the conversion of all forms of information into digital code that can be stored and shared. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “user-generated content”.

items.stem: What is the difference between “interactivity” and “digitalisation”?
items.answer: Interactivity: the ability of users to respond to and shape media content. Digitalisation: the conversion of all forms of information into digital code that can be stored and shared.

items.stem: Mohammed analysed a survey of 1200 adults in a country near Mexico City. Table: adults doing each activity in the last week (%) | Aged 16-24 | Aged 65 and over. Watched TV on demand | 84% | 52%. Posted their own content online | 69% | 25%. Listened to music by streaming | 86% | 34%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Aged 16-24 and Aged 65 and over for Listened to music by streaming (Aged 65 and over minus Aged 16-24)?
items.answer: -52 percentage points
items.markingKey: 34 − 86 = -52 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Lina, aged 16, in Mexico City watches TV series on her phone, posts her own dance videos, comments on friends’ posts and plays an online game with players in four countries. Compare how Marxist and neo-Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: new media are owned by a few huge corporations that profit from users’ data and attention; they extend capitalist control and consumerism (Fuchs). Neo-Marxism: new media spread dominant ideology in new forms, though they also give some space for counter-hegemonic voices.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Daniel analysed a survey of 1000 adults in a country near Auckland. Table: adults doing each activity in the last week (%) | Aged 16-24 | Aged 65 and over. Watched TV on demand | 84% | 52%. Posted their own content online | 68% | 31%. Listened to music by streaming | 87% | 34%. (a) Calculate the difference between Listened to music by streaming and Posted their own content online for Aged 16-24 and for Aged 65 and over, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that new media use is shaped by age.
items.answer: (a) Aged 16-24: 19 percentage points; Aged 65 and over: 3 percentage points; the difference is larger for Aged 16-24. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Aged 65 and over than for Aged 16-24 among Watched TV on demand, Posted their own content online, Listened to music by streaming; Watched TV on demand had the highest figure for Aged 65 and over. Older people may lack access or skills (digital divide). Qualifications: Older people’s use is growing quickly; survey may not include people in care homes; frequency does not show the meaning of use. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 1000 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (19 and 3); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “cultural pessimists” and “echo chamber”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Cultural pessimists: those who believe new media have harmful effects on culture, relationships and democracy (e.g. claims that social media damage mental health). Echo chamber: an online environment in which people encounter only views that reinforce their own (e.g. a news feed showing only one political view).

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research how social media affect young people’s friendships.
items.answer: Strengths: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences; they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding). Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how social media affect young people’s friendships but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A survey in Lima finds that teenagers who spend more than five hours a day on social media are more likely to report anxiety, but also that most say social media help them stay close to friends. Explain how radical feminist and Marxist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: new media reproduce patriarchy through online harassment, sexualised images and male-dominated technology industries. Marxism: new media are owned by a few huge corporations that profit from users’ data and attention; they extend capitalist control and consumerism (Fuchs).

items.stem: Arjun compared surveys of 240 adults in Bangkok about social media. Table: adults who agree with each statement (%) | 2015 | 2023. Social media make it easier to take part in politics | 56% | 45%. Social media spread false information | 49% | 73%. Social media have made my relationships stronger | 44% | 41%. (a) Calculate the gap between Social media make it easier to take part in politics and Social media have made my relationships stronger in 2015 and in 2023, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that people have become more pessimistic about new media.
items.answer: (a) 2015: 12 percentage points; 2023: 4 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Social media spread false information; the figure fell for Social media make it easier to take part in politics, Social media have made my relationships stronger; Social media spread false information had the highest figure for 2023. Experience of misinformation has increased pessimism. Qualifications: Attitudes may reflect media coverage rather than experience; agreement scales are crude; many still see benefits. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 240 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (12 and 4); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research the spread of false news stories on social media.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the spread of false news stories on social media but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: A passer-by in Lisbon films police officers using force during an arrest; the video is shared millions of times and leads to an official inquiry. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research how citizen journalists decide what to post.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how citizen journalists decide what to post but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Lina is planning a study of the amount of user-generated content on news websites. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media. Limitations: counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context; it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the amount of user-generated content on news websites but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).

items.stem: A local newspaper in Auckland closes its print edition and moves online, where readers comment on stories and send in their own photos and videos. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: new media create a media-saturated, fragmented world of choice in which people construct identities and reality blurs with representation (Baudrillard).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A national survey of 200 adults produced the results below. Table: adults doing each activity in the last week (%) | Aged 16-24 | Aged 65 and over. Watched TV on demand | 80% | 36%. Posted their own content online | 65% | 29%. Listened to music by streaming | 91% | 52%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Aged 16-24 and Aged 65 and over for Posted their own content online (Aged 65 and over minus Aged 16-24)?
items.answer: -36 percentage points
items.markingKey: 29 − 65 = -36 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A local newspaper in Doha closes its print edition and moves online, where readers comment on stories and send in their own photos and videos. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: new media are owned by a few huge corporations that profit from users’ data and attention; they extend capitalist control and consumerism (Fuchs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how young people use smartphones. Evaluate the use of participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is flexible and can uncover issues the researcher had not anticipated. Limitations: studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise; the researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”). Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how young people use smartphones but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes unequal access to new media between and within countries?
items.answer: Digital divide
items.markingKey: Digital divide: unequal access to new media between and within countries. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “echo chamber”.
items.answer: An online environment in which people encounter only views that reinforce their own.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: an online environment in which people encounter only views that reinforce their own. [1]

items.stem: Explain two pessimistic arguments about the effects of new media.
items.answer: Echo chambers and filter bubbles; misinformation; cyberbullying and mental health; surveillance and loss of privacy; corporate control of data (Fuchs); digital divide; weakened relationships (Turkle).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained argument. [4]

items.stem: Two surveys, each of 240 adults in Accra, asked about social media. Table: adults who agree with each statement (%) | 2015 | 2023. Social media make it easier to take part in politics | 56% | 50%. Social media spread false information | 54% | 75%. Social media have made my relationships stronger | 38% | 33%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Social media have made my relationships stronger change between 2015 and 2023?
items.answer: -5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 33 − 38 = -5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Mohammed compared surveys of 600 adults in Singapore about social media. Table: adults who agree with each statement (%) | 2015 | 2023. Social media make it easier to take part in politics | 51% | 45%. Social media spread false information | 47% | 72%. Social media have made my relationships stronger | 37% | 35%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for 2023. (b) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Social media spread false information between 2015 and 2023. Show your working.
items.answer: (a) Social media spread false information (72%). (b) (72 − 47) ÷ 47 × 100 = 53.2%.
items.markingKey: (a) Social media spread false information, 72%. [1] (b) 1 mark for (72 − 47) ÷ 47 × 100; 1 mark for 53.2% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying the spread of false news stories on social media.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the spread of false news stories on social media but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Two surveys, each of 600 adults in Hanoi, asked about social media. Table: adults who agree with each statement (%) | 2015 | 2023. Social media make it easier to take part in politics | 54% | 42%. Social media spread false information | 46% | 66%. Social media have made my relationships stronger | 42% | 36%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Social media have made my relationships stronger between 2015 and 2023. Show your working. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of attitudes to social media. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that people have become more pessimistic about new media.
items.answer: (a) (36 − 42) ÷ 42 × 100 = -14.3%. (b) Closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Social media spread false information; the figure fell for Social media make it easier to take part in politics, Social media have made my relationships stronger; Social media spread false information had the highest figure for 2023. Growing concerns about echo chambers and surveillance. Qualifications: Attitudes may reflect media coverage rather than experience; agreement scales are crude; many still see benefits. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (36 − 42) ÷ 42 × 100; 1 mark for -14.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the monitoring of people’s online activity and data by states or corporations?
items.answer: Digital surveillance
items.markingKey: Digital surveillance: the monitoring of people’s online activity and data by states or corporations. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Citizen journalism is produced only by professional reporters.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It is produced by members of the public.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Zuboff’s argument that tech companies profit by harvesting personal data to predict and shape behaviour, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Zuboff argued surveillance capitalism turns human experience into data for sale. Criticism: Users consent to terms of service and gain free services.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A content analysis of 400 breaking news reports on television in a country near Riyadh produced the results below. Table: share of video used in breaking news reports (%) | 2010 | 2023. Professional camera crews | 68% | 50%. Footage from members of the public | 12% | 29%. Official sources (police, government) | 20% | 21%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Footage from members of the public change between 2010 and 2023?
items.answer: +17 percentage points
items.markingKey: 29 − 12 = +17 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A free fitness app used by thousands of people in Colombo records their location, sleep and heart rate, and sells the data to advertisers and insurance companies. Explain how a pluralist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: new media spread power more widely: citizen journalism lets ordinary people challenge elites and gatekeepers, users freely choose which platforms and apps to use (trading data for free services), and regulation can protect privacy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying the sources of video used in television news.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the sources of video used in television news but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
